AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE
AbstractText.content: To describe the long-term follow-up results of complex dorsal metacarpophalangeal joint dislocation (MPJD). We hypothesize that there would be no long-term functional deficit in most patients, even with the presence of one of the familiar complications.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: We describe 5 patients with a median follow-up of 13 (range, 7-36) years and review the literature focusing on follow-up and complications.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: All patients reported full function of the hand. Compared with the contralateral finger, a mild loss of MPJ flexion was noted in 2 patients. Grip strength was reduced in 2 patients. The mean QuickDASH score was 4.5 (range, 0-20.5). Two patients with osteochondral metacarpal head fractures treated with screw fixation demonstrated secondary osteoarthritis changes on x-ray. The literature indicates that complications in patients with complex dorsal MPJD are related to failure of diagnosis, multiple attempts at closed reduction, concomitant osteochondral fracture, traumatic open reduction, or prolonged immobilization, and may result in joint stiffness, early degenerative arthritis, or osteonecrosis of the metacarpal head, pain, premature epiphysis closure, and metacarpal shortening.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: The findings from this study suggest that complex dorsal MPJD treated on the day of injury with dorsal or volar open reduction techniques can eventually result in a satisfactory outcome, even with one of the complications mentioned.
